meta.title: Who really said "Success is a lousy teacher. It seduces smart people into thinking they can't lose"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Bill Gates really wrote it: the line opens the chapter "Lessons from the Computer Industry" in The Road Ahead (Viking, 1995). A third sentence is usually cut.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Success is a lousy teacher. It seduces smart people into thinking they can't lose'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Bill Gates wrote this in The Road Ahead (Viking, 1995) — and the popular two-sentence version drops his third line.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Bill Gates, with Nathan Myhrvold and Peter Rinearson

source.excerpt: Success is a lousy teacher. It seduces smart people into thinking they can’t lose. And it’s an unreliable guide to the future. What seems the perfect business plan or latest technology today may soon be as out-of-date as the eight-track tape player, the vacuum-tube television, or the mainframe computer. I’ve watched it happen. Careful observation of many companies over a long period of time can teach you principles that will help with strategies for the years ahead.
trail: The sentence opens the excerpt from the chapter “Lessons from the Computer Industry” on roadahead.com, the book’s promotional site ↗, archived on 14 November 1996. The site’s own chapter guide ↗ confirms that heading is a chapter of the book.
Wikiquote ↗ carries the line in its sourced material, filed under the heading The Road Ahead (1995) — the same work, with no page given.

The first edition is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗ as Viking, New York, 1995, ISBN 0670772895, credited to Gates with Nathan Myhrvold and Peter Rinearson; Wikipedia ↗ dates publication to 24 November 1995. That scan is lending-restricted, so we did not read a page number off it and do not assert one.
Quote Investigator ↗ has no article on the phrase, and we found no rival claimant, no earlier attestation, and no fact-check challenging Gates’s authorship.

author.name: Bill Gates
author.heading: Who was writing
author.metaLine: b. 1955 · Microsoft co-founder · author of The Road Ahead (1995)
author.bio: Bill Gates founded Microsoft with his childhood friend Paul Allen in 1975 and ran it as chief executive for roughly its first twenty-five years, handing the job to Steve Ballmer in 2000 and resigning as chairman in February 2014. The Road Ahead, written with Microsoft technologist Nathan Myhrvold and journalist Peter Rinearson, was his first book — a 1995 forecast of what he then called the information highway. He has since written Business @ the Speed of Thought, How to Avoid a Climate Disaster, How to Prevent the Next Pandemic and the memoir Source Code: My Beginnings (2025).

misattribution.heading: What travels wrong
misattribution.intro: This is that rare thing among famous-name quotations: the name is right. Bill Gates wrote it, in a book, under his own byline. What gets mangled is the wording, the edition, and whose names belong beside his on the cover.

items.why: The passage on the book’s own excerpt page ↗ runs to three sentences: “Success is a lousy teacher. It seduces smart people into thinking they can’t lose. And it’s an unreliable guide to the future.” Almost every circulating version stops after the second. The clause that gets cut is the one that names the actual danger.

items.who: A 1996 reprint, not the 1995 first edition
items.why: AZQuotes ↗ credits the line to a 1996 edition of The Road Ahead from Wheeler Publishing. The book was first published by Viking in New York in 1995 — the edition catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗. Citing a reprint as the origin is how a date quietly drifts a year.

The Road Ahead was written by Gates with Nathan Myhrvold and Peter Rinearson, and library records name all three ↗. The sentence is published under Gates’s name and reads as his own recollection — but the book is not a solo work.

items.who: A commencement address or a keynote
items.why: The line is often introduced as something Gates said — in a speech, an interview, a graduation address. No such occasion is documented in anything we could check, and Quote Investigator has no entry ↗ on it. The only sourced home for the wording is the 1995 book.

misattribution.truthLine: He wrote it, in print, in 1995 — as the opening of the chapter “Lessons from the Computer Industry” in The Road Ahead, reproduced in the book’s own online excerpt ↗.

context.heading: Why he wrote it
lead: Gates was writing at the top of his own positive spiral. The Road Ahead reached bookshops on 24 November 1995, published by Viking; Gates was still Microsoft’s chief executive, and would remain so until Steve Ballmer took the job in 2000. The line is not modesty for its own sake — it is the opening move of a chapter arguing that the computer industry’s corpses are more instructive than its winners.

What follows the sentence makes the point concrete. Gates writes that what “seems the perfect business plan or latest technology today may soon be as out-of-date as the eight-track tape player, the vacuum-tube television, or the mainframe computer,” and adds: “I’ve watched it happen.” He then sets out the mechanism he calls the positive and the negative spiral — a hot product attracts investors, investors attract talent, talent makes the next success easier; and the same wheel turning backwards for a company that stumbles.
detailsBody: In the same excerpt Gates lists the forces he thinks explain the industry’s wreckage: “negative and positive spirals, the necessity of initiating rather than following trends, the importance of software as opposed to hardware, and the role of compatibility and the positive feedback it can generate.” He also warns that “you can’t count on conventional wisdom” in an unconventional market.

The companies he names as having gone “from nothing to a billion dollars of revenue in a flash” are Apple, Compaq, Lotus, Oracle, Sun — and Microsoft. Putting his own company on the list of beneficiaries of a spiral that can reverse is the reason the sentence still gets quoted in boardrooms.
context.pull: It seduces smart people into thinking they can’t lose.

sourcesVerified.claim: The passage "Success is a lousy teacher. It seduces smart people into thinking they can't lose. And it's an unreliable guide to the future..." appears verbatim on the book's promotional site roadahead.com under the heading "Lessons From the Computer Industry -- Bill Gates' own experiences", archived 14 November 1996.
The roadahead.com chapter guide lists 'Lessons from the Computer Industry' as a chapter of The Road Ahead, following 'A Revolution Begins' and 'The Beginning of the Information Age'.
Wikiquote lists "Success is a lousy teacher. It seduces smart people into thinking they can't lose." under a sourced section headed The Road Ahead (1995), with no page number attached to that line.

The Internet Archive record for the first edition gives: The road ahead, by Gates, Bill, 1955-; Myhrvold, Nathan; Rinearson, Peter, 1954-; publication date 1995; publisher New York: Viking; ISBN 0670772895; access-restricted item.
The Road Ahead was first published 24 November 1995 by Viking Penguin, co-authored by Bill Gates, Nathan Myhrvold and Peter Rinearson, with a revised edition in October 1996.

Bill Gates was born 28 October 1955 in Seattle, founded Microsoft with Paul Allen in 1975, served as CEO until Steve Ballmer took over in 2000, and resigned as chairman in February 2014; his books include The Road Ahead and Source Code: My Beginnings (2025).
AZQuotes attributes the quote to "Bill Gates, Nathan Myhrvold, Peter Rinearson (1996). 'The Road Ahead', Wheeler Pub Incorporated" — a 1996 edition rather than the 1995 Viking first edition.
Quote Investigator has no article on this quotation: a site search for 'lousy teacher' returns 'Nothing Found - Sorry, but nothing matched your search terms.'
LibQuotes attributes the quote to Bill Gates, The Road Ahead, 1995, without a page number.
